title: Wealth doesn't help
hook: an estate sale lays a life out on folding tables; the Buddha says carry it out of the burning house first (AN 3.52)
tomorrow: if even the body stays behind, what goes on?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the third root: only the practice helps, like a scent that travels against the wind. Today, the first thing that can't come along.

Estate sales have their own hush. A whole life laid out on folding tables: the good dishes, a coat with the tags still on, a drawer of chargers, all with little price stickers. Everything the person kept is still here. They aren't. You can't take it with you. Everyone knows the line. So what do you do with it now? The Buddha's answer came to two old men who asked him almost exactly that.
screen: `A LIFE ON FOLDING TABLES.` → `EVERYTHING KEPT IS STILL HERE.` → `SO WHAT DO YOU DO WITH IT NOW?`

segments.voice: In the Anguttara Nikaya, two brahmins, old and frail, come to the Buddha. They say they haven't done good things or built any shelter against what's coming, and they ask him to teach them. He answers with a fire. The world is burning, he says, with aging, sickness and death. When a house is on fire, the pot you carry out is the one that's useful to you, not the one that burns inside. So, since the world is burning, carry things out by giving. What's given is well carried out. That flips the estate sale. The stickers mark what stayed behind. The things that went on were given away before. The Dhammapada adds the inside view. My children, my wealth, a foolish person thinks, and is tormented; but he isn't even his own, so how can children and wealth be? None of this calls money bad. Earlier in the path, the suttas praised earning honestly and saving wisely. It only says what wealth can't do: come along. It stays behind. What goes on is what you did with it, while the house was still standing.
screen: `TWO OLD MEN ASK.` · `THE HOUSE IS ON FIRE.` · `WHAT'S GIVEN IS CARRIED OUT.` · `NOT EVEN HIS OWN.` · then, large: `IT STAYS BEHIND.`

segments.voice: Choose one thing you own that someone else would use more than you do: a book, a jacket, a spare charger. Hold it, or picture it, and set it apart right now, by the door or in a bag. Then sit with the small lightness of something already on its way out of the house.
Wealth doesn't help: at death, everything owned stays behind. What's given goes on.
The day's line: it stays behind, and what's given is carried out. Day sixteen thirty-six, lighter.

howItsDone: Giving (dana) is a central lay Buddhist practice: people give food to monks, support temples and charities, and some families make offerings in the name of a relative who has died.

fork.setup: your great-aunt is leaving everything to relatives 'after i'm gone' and gives nothing now. she asks what the burning-house sutta would say.
options: nothing; what happens after death is all that matters for giving.
give some now, while the house stands: what's given is carried out.
give everything away today and keep nothing for herself.
fork.reveal: the Buddha tells the old men to carry things out by giving, while there's still time. it's not all-or-nothing; it's now rather than later.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit: giving, generosity; how the burning-house sutta says to carry things out.

trapdoor: what you thought: you can't take it with you, so it doesn't matter.
what it means: it stays behind, but what you give while you live goes on: that's what gets carried out of the burning house.
what a scholar hears: AN 3.52 gives the two old brahmins the burning-house simile and 'what is given is well taken out'; Dhammapada 62 on 'my sons, my wealth'.
guess: possessions can't come with you when you die
being rich gets in the way of meditation
wealth can't buy friends who really care

chat.says: ông got bác Hùng's juniper. now he's giving his own bonsai away, one to me, one to the temple. worried?
options: Don't worry. He's carrying them out of the burning house while he can.
Worry. It means he thinks he's dying soon; call his doctor now.
It's just decluttering. It has nothing to do with bác Hùng.
chat.meaning: In AN 3.52 the Buddha says what's given is carried out of the burning house. Ông is giving while he's well, not waiting.

tie.story: The Buddha told two old men the world is burning, and what's given is what gets carried out.
tie.friend: Ông, seeing bác Hùng's things stay behind, is giving his trees while he can enjoy watching them go.
tie.you: what could you give now instead of 'someday'?

brahmins.meaning: members of the priestly class in the Buddha's India

Anguttara Nikaya.meaning: the collection of the Buddha's discourses arranged by number

Dhammapada.meaning: a short collection of the Buddha's sayings in verse

notes: AN 3.52 paraphrased. The sutta gives the brahmins' great age as a number; omitted (claims rule). Confirm the sutta number (AN 3.52 in PTS numbering).

'Earlier in the path, the suttas praised earning honestly and saving wisely' refers back to Block E's money days (e.g. the Sigalovada, AN 4.61); confirm those days teach this.
